definition: A transformer-based model trained on large text corpora to predict the next token. Modern LLMs (GPT-4o, Claude, Gemini, Llama) generalize to chat, reasoning, code, and tool use via instruction tuning and RLHF.
The atomic unit a language model reads and emits. Roughly 0.75 words for English; pricing, context windows, and rate limits are all token-denominated, not word-denominated.

The maximum number of tokens (input + output) the model can attend to in one request. Hitting the limit forces truncation, summarization, or retrieval. Larger windows trade cost and latency for memory.
A fixed-length numeric vector that represents the semantic meaning of text (or images, code). Similar inputs map to nearby vectors, which is what enables vector search and RAG.
A sampling parameter that controls randomness. 0 = greedy/deterministic, 1 = standard creativity, >1 = more diverse. Use low for extraction/classification, higher for brainstorming.
Sample only from the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability ≥ p. Often tuned together with temperature; lowering top-p constrains the model more than lowering temperature alone.

Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback. A fine-tuning step where the base model is aligned to human preferences via a reward model. Modern variants include DPO (Direct Preference Optimization) and Constitutional AI.

Continuing training on a smaller, task-specific dataset. Use when prompting + RAG hit a ceiling on tone, format, or domain knowledge. PEFT methods like LoRA make this cheap by training adapter weights instead of the full model.
Training a smaller, cheaper student model to mimic a larger teacher. Used to compress a stack-of-prompts pipeline into a single fine-tuned small model for production.
Constraining the model to emit valid JSON / JSON Schema / typed function arguments at decode time, not just by instruction. Eliminates an entire class of parser failures.
Including 2–8 input/output examples in the prompt to condition format and behavior. Best for shape-of-output (JSON, labels, tone). Diversify the shots — homogeneous examples cause mode collapse.
Just the instruction, no examples. Cheapest and works when the task is well-represented in pretraining (summarize, translate, extract).
Prompting the model to reason step by step before answering. Lifts accuracy on math and multi-hop tasks. Modern reasoning models do CoT internally, making explicit CoT prompts often redundant.
The high-priority instruction layer that defines persona, allowed topics, refusal style, and output format. Treated by the model as more authoritative than the user message.

Fetching relevant context from an external store (vector DB, search index, database) and prepending it to the LLM prompt. Reduces hallucination and lets the model use private/up-to-date data without retraining.
A store optimized for nearest-neighbor search over high-dimensional vectors. Implementations: Azure AI Search (vector index), Postgres + pgvector, Pinecone, Qdrant, Weaviate.
Algorithms (HNSW, IVF, ScaNN) that trade exact recall for sub-linear query time on millions+ of vectors. The recall/latency knob is the main thing to tune.
Similarity metric that compares the angle between two vectors (1 = identical direction, 0 = orthogonal). The default for most embedding models; some prefer dot product or Euclidean.
Combining BM25 / keyword search with vector search and merging results (RRF or learned). Beats either signal alone — keywords nail exact terms, vectors handle paraphrase.
A second-stage cross-encoder that re-scores the top-k retrieved chunks given the query. Usually lifts answer quality more than swapping the base embedding model.
Splitting source documents into retrieval units. Strategy (fixed token / sentence / semantic / structural) materially affects retrieval quality. Overlap reduces boundary loss.
Anchoring an LLM response in retrieved or tool-provided context, ideally with citations. The primary mitigation for hallucination.
Confidently stated output that is not supported by the input or by reality. Caused by missing context, stale parametric knowledge, or format pressure that forces invention.

An LLM-driven loop that observes state, decides on an action (often a tool call), executes it, and feeds the result back into the next step. Adds non-determinism and cost vs a single prompt — use only when needed.
Letting the model call typed functions (search, code-exec, DB queries, APIs) with structured arguments. The 'function calling' / 'tools' API on most providers is the production-grade interface.
A prompting pattern that interleaves Reason and Act steps so the model verbalizes its plan before each tool call. Easy to debug; can be replaced by graph-based orchestration in production.
A library that takes care of agent plumbing: tool registration, state, retries, traces, multi-agent orchestration. Examples: Microsoft Agent Framework, LangGraph, Semantic Kernel, AutoGen.
An open protocol for exposing tools, resources, and prompts to an LLM client over a standard JSON-RPC transport. Lets one server be reused across many agent hosts (Claude, Copilot, custom).

Measuring LLM application quality on a fixed set of inputs with a defined rubric. Combines exact-match / regex (deterministic), LLM-as-judge (qualitative), and behavioral metrics (refusal, latency, cost).
A curated, version-controlled set of input/expected-output pairs used to gate prompt and model changes. Should cover happy paths, edge cases, and known regressions.
Using a (usually larger) LLM to score responses against a rubric (faithfulness, helpfulness, tone). Cheaper than human review at scale; needs calibration against humans periodically.
How well an answer is supported by the provided context. Distinct from helpfulness — an answer can be helpful but unfaithful (or faithful but unhelpful).
Evaluating an agent on the path it took (tool selection, argument quality, recovery), not just the final answer. Reveals lucky-success vs robust behavior.
Attacker text that overrides the model's intended behavior. Direct = user types it; indirect = model reads it from a web page, email, or RAG chunk. Indirect is the dominant agent-era risk.
A prompt that bypasses safety training to elicit refused content. Defenses: prompt shields, system-prompt hardening, output filtering, refusal-rate monitoring.

Filtering input and output for harmful categories (hate, sexual, violence, self-harm) plus jailbreak / prompt-injection patterns. Azure AI Content Safety provides categorical scores plus Prompt Shields.

End-to-end practices for fair, safe, transparent AI: harm assessments, content safety, PII handling, audit logs, user reporting, and red-teaming. Microsoft's RAI Standard is one widely cited reference.
Runtime checks around an LLM that block, redact, or rewrite unsafe inputs/outputs and constrain tool use. Layered with model-side safety, not a substitute for it.
Per-call observability: prompt version, model, tokens in/out, latency, cost, outcome, user feedback. The foundation for diagnosing regressions and reporting on quality.
A runtime switch that gates a code path (new prompt, new model, new tool) so it can be rolled out gradually and rolled back without a deploy.
Routing a small slice (1–5%) of traffic to a new version, watching paired metrics, and ramping gradually. Reduces blast radius on prompt/model changes.
Treating prompts as production artifacts: versioned in git, evaluated in CI on a golden set, rolled out behind a flag, observed in production.
An Entra ID identity attached to an Azure resource so it can authenticate to other services without secrets. Pair with RBAC to grant least-privilege access (e.g., Storage Blob Data Reader).
Azure-hosted OpenAI models (GPT, embeddings, Whisper, image) with VNet integration, content safety, customer-managed keys, and regional residency. Same API surface as OpenAI.
Managed search service with BM25 + vector + semantic ranking + integrated vectorization. The default RAG index for Azure-native solutions.
Microsoft's unified platform for building, evaluating, and operating AI apps and agents — model catalog, projects, hosted agents, evaluation, tracing, content safety.
Returning model output token-by-token over SSE or chunked HTTP so the user sees progress. Reduces perceived latency; requires care with proxy buffering and parser-tolerant rendering.
A one-way text/event-stream HTTP transport. The simplest production transport for streaming LLM responses to a browser. Disable proxy buffering or chunks queue up.
Property where repeated requests produce the same effect as a single request. Critical for retries, queue consumers, and webhooks. Implement with an idempotency key + a dedupe store.
A side queue that captures messages that failed processing after their max delivery attempts. Inspect, fix, and replay; never silently drop.
Microsoft's five pillars for cloud workloads: Reliability, Security, Cost Optimization, Operational Excellence, Performance Efficiency. Use as a checklist when reviewing or designing.
Proving who a principal is. Mechanisms: passwords + MFA, federated SSO (OIDC/SAML), client certs, mTLS, API keys. Outputs proof — a session, a JWT, or a TLS-verified identity.

Deciding what an authenticated principal is allowed to do on which resource. Models include RBAC (roles), ABAC (attributes/policy), and ReBAC (relationships). Always evaluated server-side, on the resource.

Standard for delegated authorization — a third-party app obtains a scoped, expiring access token to call an API on a user's behalf, without ever seeing the user's password. Modern flows: Authorization Code + PKCE, Client Credentials, On-Behalf-Of, Device Code.
Authentication layer built on OAuth 2.0. Adds an ID token (JWT describing the user) and standard discovery (`.well-known/openid-configuration`) so apps can verify *who* signed in.

Extension to OAuth Authorization Code flow that prevents authorization-code interception. The client generates a code verifier + challenge; only the verifier can redeem the code. Mandatory for public clients (SPAs, mobile, native).

A signed, base64url-encoded `header.payload.signature` token used to convey identity and claims. Validation must check signature, algorithm (pinned), issuer, audience, and expiry — never trust the payload alone.

A public endpoint published by an OIDC issuer (`/.well-known/jwks.json`) listing the public keys used to sign JWTs. Clients fetch and cache keys; the JWT's `kid` header selects the right one. Enables zero-downtime key rotation.
A short-lived credential (typically 60–90 min) presented to a resource server to prove the caller is authorized for a specific scope. Often a JWT in OIDC ecosystems; opaque per the OAuth spec.
OIDC-defined JWT that describes the authenticated user (`sub`, `name`, `email`). Consumed by the *client* to know who signed in — not used to call APIs (that's the access token).

Long-lived credential used to obtain new access tokens without re-prompting the user. Must be stored securely, rotated on every use, and revocation-checked. Refresh-token reuse detection should invalidate the entire token family.

Any token whose mere possession authorizes the caller — `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. Whoever holds it can use it, so transport security (HTTPS), short lifetimes, and safe storage are non-negotiable.

OAuth flow where a service that received a user's access token exchanges it for a new token to call a downstream API *as that user*. Preserves user identity and per-user permissions through service chains.

Named permission requested by an OAuth client (`Mail.Read`, `https://cognitiveservices.azure.com/.default`). Granted via user or admin consent and embedded in the access token. Resource servers enforce scopes per operation.

A statement carried inside a token — `iss`, `aud`, `exp`, `sub`, `tid`, `roles`, custom app claims. Authorization decisions read claims; security depends on validating the token before trusting any claim.

Authorization model that assigns permissions via roles (e.g., `Reader`, `Contributor`, `Cognitive Services OpenAI User`) at a scope (management group → subscription → resource group → resource). Inherits downward; assign at the narrowest scope.

Trust an external OIDC issuer (GitHub Actions, AWS, GitLab, AKS) so its short-lived tokens can be exchanged for Azure access tokens — eliminating stored client secrets in CI/CD and external workloads.

Azure SDK credential that walks an ordered chain (env vars → workload identity → managed identity → CLI/VS) until one returns a token. Convenient for local-dev-to-prod parity; pin to a specific credential in production for predictability.

The global definition of an application in Entra ID — client id, redirect URIs, exposed scopes, requested API permissions, federated credentials. Distinct from the *enterprise application* (service principal), which is the per-tenant instance.

App-setting syntax (`@Microsoft.KeyVault(SecretUri=...)`) that lets App Service / Functions / Container Apps read a secret from Key Vault at runtime via Managed Identity, instead of storing the raw value in config.
